_**The Fosters**_ is an American [family drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_(film_and_television) "Drama (film and television)") television series created by [Peter Paige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Paige "Peter Paige") and Bradley Bredeweg. It premiered in the United States on June 3, 2013, on the ABC Family (later [Freeform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeform_(TV_channel) "Freeform (TV channel)")) television network and concluded on June 6, 2018. It follows the lives of the Adams-Foster family led by a lesbian couple, Stef Foster, a [police officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_officer "Police officer"), and Lena Adams, a school [vice principal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_principal "Vice principal"), who raise one biological son and four adopted teenagers in [San Diego, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego "San Diego").

The first season received generally favorable reviews and particular acclaim for its portrayal of [LGBT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT "LGBT") themes. It also earned two [GLAAD Media Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLAAD_Media_Awards "GLAAD Media Awards") and one [Teen Choice Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teen_Choice_Awards "Teen Choice Awards").

On January 3, 2018, Freeform announced that _The Fosters_ would end after five seasons. It concluded with a three-episode finale, which also acted as an introduction to _[Good Trouble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good\_Trouble\_(TV\_series) "Good Trouble (TV series)")_, the spin-off series starring [Maia Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maia_Mitchell "Maia Mitchell") and [Cierra Ramirez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cierra_Ramirez "Cierra Ramirez").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-1)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

This five season series follows the lives of the Adams Foster family who live in San Diego. The matriarchal heads of this family are police officer Stef Foster and her life partner Lena Adams, a school vice principal. Their multiethnic, blended family includes Brandon, Stef's biological son from her previous marriage, and twins Jesus and Mariana, who were adopted as children. The series begins when the couple take in two foster children, siblings Callie and Jude Jacobs, whom they later adopt. The five children have rough times navigating adolescence because of poor life choices.

Also part of their lives is Mike Foster, Stef's patrol partner and ex-husband, and Brandon's biological father.

Most of the show takes place at the family's craftsman-style home in the quiet San Diego suburb of Mission Bay and at Anchor Beach Community Charter School.

### Main

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Main")]

*   Stef Adams Foster ([Teri Polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teri_Polo "Teri Polo"))[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-B-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3) is Lena's wife, Brandon's biological mother, and the adoptive mother to twins Jesus and Mariana. In the pilot episode, she and Lena also [foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fostering "Fostering") Callie Jacob, and later her younger maternal [half-brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-brother "Half-brother") Jude, whom they will subsequently [adopt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adoption "Adoption"). Stef is a police officer for the [San Diego Police Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_Police_Department "San Diego Police Department"), where she works as a patrol partner with Brandon's biological father and her ex-husband, Mike. She is known for having a strong personality with bold opinions but can also be loving and motherly. When Jesus goes missing one night, Mariana informs her parents how she fears Jesus is at their biological mother Ana's house since they recently got in contact and have been lending her money. Stef and Mike go to rescue Jesus only to discover that he is not there, and Ana's boyfriend, an abusive drug addict, shoots Stef, who is severely wounded before making a full recovery. Later, she officially marries Lena, and after having a [mammogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammography "Mammography"), Stef receives a diagnosis of [intraductal carcinoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ductal_carcinoma_in_situ "Ductal carcinoma in situ"). Because it is likely that the cells will become cancerous, she undergoes surgery.
*   Lena Adams Foster ([Sherri Saum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherri_Saum "Sherri Saum"))[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-A-4) is Stef's wife, step-mother to Brandon, and adoptive mother to Jesus and Mariana. In the pilot episode, she and Lena also [foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fostering "Fostering") Callie Jacob, and later her younger maternal [half-brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sibling "Sibling") Jude, whom they will subsequently [adopt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adoption "Adoption"). Lena is the vice principal of Anchor Beach Community Charter School, the [high school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_school "Secondary school") her children attend. She tends to be more open and reasonable, oftentimes when it comes to the children's wrongdoings but can be stern as well. She and Stef legally marry, and the discussion of Lena carrying her first child arises. Lena interviews for a promotion at work and reveals she is pregnant, leading the panel to question her ability to balance work and home. She later develops [Pre-eclampsia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-eclampsia "Pre-eclampsia"), which leads to a [miscarriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miscarriage "Miscarriage").
*   Callie Adams Foster (formerly Callie Quinn Jacob) ([Maia Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maia_Mitchell "Maia Mitchell"))[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast2-5) is the adoptive daughter of Stef and Lena, adoptive sister to Brandon, Mariana, and Jesus, and maternal half-sister to Jude. In the pilot episode, the court places Callie in the Adams Foster home after serving time in juvenile detention for damaging her abusive foster father's property. Later, with Brandon's help, she goes to get her younger half-brother Jude (then believed to be her brother), who is still in the abusive foster home. Callie quickly develops a crush on Brandon before Jude becomes furious at her after seeing them kiss at Stef and Lena's wedding. Fearing the court will place her back into foster care, Callie attempts to run away, where she ends up eating food at a gas station without paying. This leads her into a temporary group home to counsel her actions and keep her away from Brandon. As time passes, Callie and Brandon hold back their feelings for each other. Callie's adoption is initially put on hold after the discovery that she and Jude do not share the same birth father. Later, Robert Quinn, who reveals himself to be Callie's birth father, approaches Callie. Robert introduces her to his family, and she quickly bonds with his daughter, Sophia. After Robert feels ready to turn over his paternal rights, Sophia tears up the paperwork, hoping Callie feels the same way about their newfound sibling bond, which appears to be the exact opposite. Stef and Lena officially adopt her following a prolonged battle with the justice system and a passionate speech to the judge.
*   Mariana Adams Foster ([Cierra Ramirez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cierra_Ramirez "Cierra Ramirez"))[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3) is Stef and Lena's adoptive daughter, Jesus' twin sister, younger adoptive sister to Brandon and Callie, and Jude's older adoptive sister. Mariana is an intelligent teenage girl who likes to involve herself in whatever she finds enjoyable, particularly when she is social with her friends and gossips at school. She is also very proficient at coding and mathematics. Like many teenage girls, Mariana struggles with her self-confidence, heritage, and appearance, as seen when she dyes her hair blond to fit in. She dances, acts, sings, and eventually forms her own dance team before becoming the lead actress in Brandon's senior project musical. Mariana initially supports her birth mother financially by selling Jesus' ADHD medication at school. Jesus confronts their birth mom to no longer contact Mariana, only to also rope in Brandon, which causes him financial and physical harm, for which she is apologetic. Later, Mariana hopes to change her image, joins the dance team, and takes a liking toward one of Brandon's bandmates. She is very close to Jesus, but they often tease each other.
*   Jesus Adams Foster ([Jake T. Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jake_T._Austin "Jake T. Austin") in seasons 1–2, [Noah Centineo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noah_Centineo "Noah Centineo") in seasons 3–5)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast2-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-6) is Stef and Lena's adoptive son, twin brother to Mariana, and adoptive sibling to Brandon, Callie, and Jude. He has [ADHD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADHD "ADHD") and joins the wrestling team in an effort to offset the negative effects of his medication through the advice of Mike. Jesus loves his twin sister, Mariana, and the pair share resentment toward their biological mother. He is a womanizer at first, having a short string of romantic relationships and sometimes charming his mothers, including when he covers up for Mariana's wrongdoings. But he is now more respectful after getting back together with Emma. Jesus feels as though he has no involvement in Mariana's [quinceañera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincea%C3%B1era "Quinceañera") preparations but later opts to be her escort in an effort to be at their birthday celebration. In the third season, Jesus temporarily resides at a boarding school for his high school wrestling team but returns after Callie's adoption. After he admits to his parents that he was taking [steroids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steroids "Steroids") while away at boarding school, Stef and Lena no longer allow Jesus to participate on the wrestling team at Anchor Beach. Jesus later suffers a [TBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traumatic_brain_injury "Traumatic brain injury") after accidentally shooting himself in the head with a nail gun, which affects his personality and his academic performance.
*   Jude Adams Foster (formerly Jude Jacob) ([Hayden Byerly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayden_Byerly "Hayden Byerly"))[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast2-5) is the youngest Adams Foster child, he is Callie's half brother, and he is also Brandon, Jesus, and Mariana's adoptive sibling. Callie rescues Jude from their abusive foster father's house. As Jude settles into his new home, Mariana paints his nails blue and Callie tells him to wash it off but then learns to accept Jude's choices. At school, he quickly becomes friends with a kind-hearted boy, Connor, and as their friendship grows, Jude begins [questioning his sexual orientation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Questioning_(sexuality_and_gender) "Questioning (sexuality and gender)").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Hollywood_Life-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Hollywood.com-8) When Connor's father suspects Jude's feelings, he forbids the boys from seeing each other outside of school. Jude slips into a phase of [selective mutism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selective_mutism "Selective mutism"), a [social anxiety disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_anxiety_disorder "Social anxiety disorder") where he does not speak entirely for a certain extent of time in fear of embarrassment, only to finally open up to Callie about his feelings. Jude and Connor kiss and begin dating, but Jude refuses to label himself as gay. After seeing how badly this affects Connor at an LGBTQ dance in season 3, he [comes out as gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_out "Coming out"). At the end of the first season, Stef and Lena legally adopt Jude. Following Callie's own adoption, Jude admits he is in love with Connor, who returns the sentiment. After Connor moves to [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") to live with his mom and because their long-distance relationship does not work out very well, they break up, and he later dates a new friend, Noah. Jude finally graduates from ABCC and gets into the College of Arts and Letters, UCLA. He and Noah maintain their relationship throughout their high school years, but break up when Noah goes to university, although they remain good friends.
*   Brandon Foster ([David Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lambert_(actor) "David Lambert (actor)"))[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast2-5) is the eldest Foster child, biological son of Stef and Mike, and older adoptive brother to Jesus and Mariana, as well as to Callie and Jude. Brandon has an infatuation for Callie but after his biological mother and father place a [restraining order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restraining_order "Restraining order") against him, and despite he and Callie having sex the night before her adoption, they later resist further temptations to proceed with their relationship. Brandon also has a talent for music, excelling in piano, and is on the verge of entering a highly distinguished music program. After raising money to obtain fake IDs to get into a bar (as he is legally underage), Brandon is beat up by his dealer. Following his subsequent hospitalization, Brandon loses sensation in his hand, causing him to miss his spot in the music program. Still able to play the piano, he joins a band. In the third season, Brandon goes to the Idylwild band camp and competes to play at [Disney Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney_Hall "Disney Hall"), where he wins the competition. During his senior year of high school, he receives an acceptance letter into [The Juilliard School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Juilliard_School "The Juilliard School"), his top choice in colleges and among the most prestigious in music and the arts. Later, however, Brandon is [academically dismissed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academically_dismissed "Academically dismissed") from ever attending college as a student discloses bribing Brandon to take his [scholastic assessment test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAT "SAT").
*   Mike Foster ([Danny Nucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Nucci "Danny Nucci"))[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast2-5) is Stef's patrol partner and ex-husband as well as Brandon's father. He makes a number of appearances in the Adams Foster home, especially when it involves seeing Brandon. When searching for Jesus in the twins' birth mother's home, Mike witnesses Ana's boyfriend shooting Stef and, in turn, Mike fires at the shooter. Mike hadn't noticed the shooter dropped the gun and still shot him, which Stef witnessed, forcing her to hide the truth to protect Mike. He later learns that the money he gives his son for piano lessons is used to bribe Ana to lie in court so Mike does not lose his job. This only complicates the issue as the court abruptly determines that Mike is not guilty before Ana even has the chance to testify. Mike is also a recovering alcoholic, attends [Alcoholics Anonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholics_Anonymous "Alcoholics Anonymous") meetings, and retains a live-in girlfriend, Dani, who helps maintain his sobriety. The pair break up when she is sent to prison for [statutory rape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statutory_rape "Statutory rape") with an already sober Brandon. Mike and Ana soon begin a romantic relationship and get engaged in season 5 and the two got married during the time jump; he also becomes the step-father of Bella. Mike was also the foster father to AJ Hensdale.

## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Production")]

### Conception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Conception")]

_The Fosters_ was originally conceived by [openly gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Openly_gay "Openly gay") creators Bradley Bredeweg and [Peter Paige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Paige "Peter Paige")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-TheBacklot1-11) who wanted to write a drama that reflected the "modern American family". After originally considering a story about two gay fathers, the pair decided the subject of two men raising a family had already been done on television and began to instead consider a story about two women.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HuffPostGV1-12) When asked about the concept of two lesbian mothers raising a blended family, Bredeweg stated, "We realized that there was a kind of a vacuum when it came to stories about women raising families. So we set off in that direction. Many of our own friends are moms raising biological kids. Some of them have fostered and adopted. Suddenly, we realized that we had a story here that hadn't been told on television before."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HuffPostGV1-12) Additionally, certain elements of the series which deal with the foster care system are said to have been inspired by a troubled childhood friend of Bredeweg, who struggled in the foster system before eventually being adopted in her senior year of high school.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HuffPostGV1-12)

### Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Development")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Jennifer_Lopez_at_GLAAD_Media_Awards.jpg/250px-Jennifer_Lopez_at_GLAAD_Media_Awards.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jennifer_Lopez_at_GLAAD_Media_Awards.jpg)

Executive producer [Jennifer Lopez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Lopez "Jennifer Lopez")

When developing the concept, Bredeweg and Paige were initially met with some resistance from Hollywood, with Bredeweg recounting, "[T]here were some people around us, some people in town who said, 'You know, it is just not going to happen. You are never going to sell this show.'" After completing the first draft of the pilot script, the team was introduced to [Jennifer Lopez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Lopez "Jennifer Lopez") through a friend who worked at her production company [Nuyorican Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuyorican_Productions "Nuyorican Productions"), which was looking to branch out into scripted television. When describing their initial pitch to Lopez, Bredeweg stated, "When we met with Jennifer, she really fell in love with it. The moment we had her, we knew that we had a force behind us."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HuffPostGV1-12)

Lopez's decision to become involved in the project is said to have been largely inspired by her late Aunt Marisa, Lopez's mother's gay elder sister who had faced discrimination during her lifetime due to her sexual orientation and was unable to have a family of her own.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HollywoodReporter2-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-UsWeekly-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-EntertainmentTonight-15) When discussing the show's concept, Lopez stated, "Although [the script] was about a non-traditional family and had some newer themes, it had some really basic themes as well about family and love and what's really important. And life can be complicated and messy sometimes and not simple. It gives a really good depiction of family in this day and age."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-EntertainmentTonight-15)

With Lopez on board, the team took the concept to several networks, including ABC Family, with Bredeweg recalling, "ABC Family was really receptive from the very beginning. Strangely, it felt a little like a match made in heaven. I mean, their slogan is 'A new kind of family.' We had a new kind of modern family, and it took off from there."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HuffPostGV1-12) On July 6, 2012, _[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hollywood\_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter"),_ among other sources, reported that Jennifer Lopez and her production company, Nuyorican Productions, were developing the yet-to-be-titled hour-long drama for ABC Family, with Lopez set to executive produce alongside [Simon Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Fields "Simon Fields") and Greg Gugliotta, as well as [showrunners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Showrunner "Showrunner") and head writers Peter Paige and Brad Bredeweg.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-17)

Finally, the first televised promo appeared on ABC Family on April 19, 2013.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Philly-18)

### Casting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Casting")]

On August 23, 2012, sources reported that ABC Family had ordered a pilot for _The Fosters_, a series which would tell the story of a lesbian couple raising a "21st-century" multi-ethnic mix of foster and biological children.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HollywoodReporter3-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-21) On September 24, 2012, it was reported that [Teri Polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teri_Polo "Teri Polo") and [Sherri Saum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherri_Saum "Sherri Saum") had been cast to star in the pilot as the two leads, Stef Adams Foster and Lena Adams Foster, respectively.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Deadline.com1-22) It is worth noting that neither are openly members of the LGBTQ+ community.

On February 6, 2013, it was reported that ABC Family had picked up the show, with production set to begin that spring for a summer 2013 premiere. The rest of the principal cast was also announced at that time, including [Danny Nucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Nucci "Danny Nucci") as Stef's ex-husband Mike Foster, [David Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lambert_(actor) "David Lambert (actor)") as their biological son Brandon Foster, [Jake T. Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jake_T._Austin "Jake T. Austin") and [Cierra Ramirez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cierra_Ramirez "Cierra Ramirez") as Stef and Lena's twins Jesus and Mariana Foster, and [Maia Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maia_Mitchell "Maia Mitchell") and [Hayden Byerly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayden_Byerly "Hayden Byerly") as their foster children Callie and Jude Jacob.

When recounting the casting process, Bredeweg explained, "[W]e spent tireless hours trying to find the right person for each role. Then they all began to line up—it was like dominos—the moment we found our Lena, the moment we found our Callie, the moment we found our Stef, it sort of all started to line up perfectly for us."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HuffPostGV1-12) On April 11, 2013, _[TV Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV\_Guide "TV Guide")_ unveiled the first official cast photo of _The Fosters_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-23)

In March 2015, it was announced that Jake T. Austin would be leaving the show. He tweeted: "I'm honored to have been a part of such a groundbreaking series, but I personally want to let you know that my time on the show has come to an end. Thank you for letting me be a part of your family, it's been a pleasure." It was announced three months later that [Noah Centineo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noah_Centineo "Noah Centineo") would replace Austin in the role of Jesus.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-AccessHollywood1-24)

## Broadcast

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Broadcast")]

_The Fosters_ premiered on June 3, 2013, and ran for ten episodes. On July 30, 2013, the series was picked up for a full season[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-25) and an additional eleven episodes were produced,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-extraepisodes-26) with the first season returning on January 13, 2014, before concluding on March 24. On October 11, 2013, ABC Family renewed _The Fosters_ for a second season[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-secondhalfpremiere-29) that premiered on June 16, 2014. The summer finale premiered on August 18, 2014. In July, ABC Family announced a Christmas special to premiere in December with the second half of season 2 to premiere in January 2015. The third season premiered on June 8, 2015.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-S3P-30)

On January 13, 2015, ABC Family renewed the series for a third season which premiered on June 8,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-S3P-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-31) with the second half set to premiere on January 18, 2016, on _Freeform_.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-32) On November 24, 2015, the premiere date was pushed to a week later on January 25, 2016.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-33) On November 30, 2015, ABC Family announced that _The Fosters_ was renewed for a fourth season and began airing on June 20, 2016.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-34)

While Canada broadcasts the series on [ABC Spark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Spark "ABC Spark"), it airs on [Fox8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox8 "Fox8") in Australia where its second season premiered on February 3, 2015.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-35) In Turkey, the series airs on _Dizimax Drama_.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-36)

On January 10, 2017, The Fosters was renewed for a fifth season, which included the series' 100th episode.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-37)

On January 3, 2018, Freeform announced that _The Fosters_ was ending after five seasons. The show's two-hour 100th episode acted as a Season 5 finale, setting up the three-part limited series event that aired in June 2018. The three-episode finale will introduce a spin-off series centered around Maia Mitchell's Callie and Cierra Ramirez's Mariana.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-38)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Critical reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Critical reception")]

On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), _The Fosters_ received an overall score of 98%.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-40) On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), the first season of the show holds a score of 69 out of 100, based on twelve reviews, indicating "generally favorable reviews".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Metacritic-41)

While acknowledging its network was somewhat beholden to the "soapy" format its target demographic had become accustomed to, critics praised the series for its ability to appeal to adults and younger viewers alike, with _[Boston Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston\_Herald "Boston Herald")_ critic Mark A. Perigard writing, "The show cannily plays to teen hopes and dreams [...] but there's story for the adults as well."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-BostonHerald-42)_[St. Louis Post-Dispatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St.\_Louis\_Post-Dispatch "St. Louis Post-Dispatch")_ critic Gail Pennington echoed the sentiment, writing "Intelligent enough for adults, accessible enough for younger viewers and entertaining enough for both."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Post-Dispatch-43)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Sherri_Saum_and_Teri_Polo.jpg/330px-Sherri_Saum_and_Teri_Polo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sherri_Saum_and_Teri_Polo.jpg)

Series stars Sherri Saum and Teri Polo

The series has garnered positive reception for its innovative portrayal of [LGBT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT "LGBT") characters and themes. _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment\_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_ critic, Sarah Caldwell wrote that "[s]eeing a lesbian, biracial couple on a family TV show is a big deal. [I]f you look at the demographics of most TV shows, it's easy to realize how important, and deliberate, this choice was."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-EntertainmentWeekly-44)_[Philadelphia Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia\_Daily\_News "Philadelphia Daily News")_ critic Ellen Gray wrote, "Stef and Lena [are] the kind of parents I've met more in real life than on television. I hope they'll be as welcome there as they seem to be welcoming."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Philly.com-45)[TV Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_Guide "TV Guide") critic Matt Rousch felt similarly, writing, "there's something refreshing about its unforced approach to redefining what a family looks like."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-TV_Guide-46) In addition to its adult characters, the series garnered praise for its handling of 13-year-old Jude's [questioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Questioning_(sexuality_and_gender) "Questioning (sexuality and gender)") of his [sexual orientation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_orientation "Sexual orientation"), with [Hollywood.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood.com "Hollywood.com") citing Byerly's "heartwarming" portrayal when naming Jude to its list of "Favorite LGBTQ Characters on TV" in 2014.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Hollywood.com-8) The LGBT advocacy organization [GLAAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLAAD "GLAAD") and gay-interest media outlet [TheBacklot.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TheBacklot.com "TheBacklot.com") also commended the show's decision to introduce the character of [transgender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender "Transgender") teenager Cole, portrayed by transgender actor Tom Phelan, in the second half of its first season.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-TheBacklot1-11)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-GLAAD1-47)

In his review of the pilot episode, _[Variety's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ Brian Lowry criticized what he felt were formulaic elements, writing that what was distinctive about the series appeared to have been "extracted during the pitch meeting, indicating a show either built by committee or incorporating too many notes." Although acknowledging that Polo and Saum were competent actresses and that the show "had its heart in the right place", Lowry described the series as an "utterly by-the-numbers affair".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Variety1-48)_[PopMatters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PopMatters "PopMatters")_ critic Maysa Hattab detected some of the same problems, writing "_[T]he Fosters_ feel less like a family than a careful assembly of machine-tooled parts, as if the show were engineered for a focus group approved 'family drama' category", while conceding that the lead characters, Stef and Lena were "a likeable pair".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-PopMatters-49)

#### Controversy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Controversy")]

On October 8, 2012, more than seven months prior to the series debut, the socially conservative [One Million Moms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Million_Moms "One Million Moms") organization, a division of the [American Family Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Family_Association "American Family Association"), condemned Lopez and the show, encouraging audiences to boycott it.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-EntertainmentWeekly2-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-ABC-51) The group, which has routinely advocated against the depiction of same-sex couples in the media, stated: "While foster care and adoption is a wonderful thing and the Bible does teach us to help orphans, this program is attempting to redefine marriage and family by having two moms raise these children together."[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-53) They issued the following statement:

Obviously, ABC has lost their minds. They haven't let up so neither will we. ABC's Family Channel has several anti-family programs, and they are planning on adding to that growing list. ABC Family has approved a series pilot from Jennifer Lopez's production company, Nuyorican, about a lesbian couple and their diverse family.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-ABC-51)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-55)
In response, ABC defended the television show, with ABC Family President [Michael Riley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Riley "Michael Riley") countering that _The Fosters_ merges perfectly with the network's "groundbreaking storytelling and iconic characters" and will feature "the same depth, heart, close relationships and authenticity that our viewers have come to expect".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-56) Other sources have also defended the show. Josh Middleton, a writer from _[Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia\_(magazine) "Philadelphia (magazine)")_ magazine, called One Million Moms' statement "silliness" as well as "ridiculous" and said, "They obviously missed the boat on shows like _[Modern Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern\_Family "Modern Family")_ and _[The New Normal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Normal\_(TV\_series) "The New Normal (TV series)")_, which have been on air—and killing it in the ratings game—for a while now".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Philly-18)

## Spin-off

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Spin-off")]

Main article: [_Good Trouble_ (TV series)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Trouble_(TV_series) "Good Trouble (TV series)")

On January 3, 2018, following the announcement of the ending of the series, Freeform announced a spin-off was in the works. It would center the lives of Callie and Mariana Adams Foster, now living in Los Angeles, a few years after the series finale of _The Fosters_, which contains a five-year time jump. The spin-off was given a 13-episode order.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-86) On May 23, 2018, it was announced that the title of the spin-off series was _Good Trouble_.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-87) On February 5, 2019, it was announced via Twitter that the show has been renewed for a second season.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-88) On January 17, 2020, the series has been renewed for a third season.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-S3Renewal-89) The renewal for the fourth season was announced on September 8, 2021. The fourth season premiered on March 9, 2022 on freeform, and on March 10 on Hulu.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-90) The fifth and final season aired in two parts.

_**The Fosters**_ is an American [family drama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drama_(film_and_television) "Drama (film and television)") television series created by [Peter Paige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Paige "Peter Paige") and Bradley Bredeweg. It premiered in the United States on June 3, 2013, on the ABC Family (later [Freeform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeform_(TV_channel) "Freeform (TV channel)")) television network and concluded on June 6, 2018. It follows the lives of the Adams-Foster family led by a lesbian couple, Stef Foster, a [police officer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Police_officer "Police officer"), and Lena Adams, a school [vice principal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vice_principal "Vice principal"), who raise one biological son and four adopted teenagers in [San Diego, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego "San Diego").

The first season received generally favorable reviews and particular acclaim for its portrayal of [LGBT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT "LGBT") themes. It also earned two [GLAAD Media Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLAAD_Media_Awards "GLAAD Media Awards") and one [Teen Choice Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teen_Choice_Awards "Teen Choice Awards").

On January 3, 2018, Freeform announced that _The Fosters_ would end after five seasons. It concluded with a three-episode finale, which also acted as an introduction to _[Good Trouble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good\_Trouble\_(TV\_series) "Good Trouble (TV series)")_, the spin-off series starring [Maia Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maia_Mitchell "Maia Mitchell") and [Cierra Ramirez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cierra_Ramirez "Cierra Ramirez").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-1)

## Plot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Plot")]

This five season series follows the lives of the Adams Foster family who live in San Diego. The matriarchal heads of this family are police officer Stef Foster and her life partner Lena Adams, a school vice principal. Their multiethnic, blended family includes Brandon, Stef's biological son from her previous marriage, and twins Jesus and Mariana, who were adopted as children. The series begins when the couple take in two foster children, siblings Callie and Jude Jacobs, whom they later adopt. The five children have rough times navigating adolescence because of poor life choices.

Also part of their lives is Mike Foster, Stef's patrol partner and ex-husband, and Brandon's biological father.

Most of the show takes place at the family's craftsman-style home in the quiet San Diego suburb of Mission Bay and at Anchor Beach Community Charter School.

### Main

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Main")]

*   Stef Adams Foster ([Teri Polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teri_Polo "Teri Polo"))[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-B-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3) is Lena's wife, Brandon's biological mother, and the adoptive mother to twins Jesus and Mariana. In the pilot episode, she and Lena also [foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fostering "Fostering") Callie Jacob, and later her younger maternal [half-brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half-brother "Half-brother") Jude, whom they will subsequently [adopt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adoption "Adoption"). Stef is a police officer for the [San Diego Police Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_Police_Department "San Diego Police Department"), where she works as a patrol partner with Brandon's biological father and her ex-husband, Mike. She is known for having a strong personality with bold opinions but can also be loving and motherly. When Jesus goes missing one night, Mariana informs her parents how she fears Jesus is at their biological mother Ana's house since they recently got in contact and have been lending her money. Stef and Mike go to rescue Jesus only to discover that he is not there, and Ana's boyfriend, an abusive drug addict, shoots Stef, who is severely wounded before making a full recovery. Later, she officially marries Lena, and after having a [mammogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammography "Mammography"), Stef receives a diagnosis of [intraductal carcinoma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ductal_carcinoma_in_situ "Ductal carcinoma in situ"). Because it is likely that the cells will become cancerous, she undergoes surgery.
*   Lena Adams Foster ([Sherri Saum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherri_Saum "Sherri Saum"))[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-A-4) is Stef's wife, step-mother to Brandon, and adoptive mother to Jesus and Mariana. In the pilot episode, she and Lena also [foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fostering "Fostering") Callie Jacob, and later her younger maternal [half-brother](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sibling "Sibling") Jude, whom they will subsequently [adopt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adoption "Adoption"). Lena is the vice principal of Anchor Beach Community Charter School, the [high school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secondary_school "Secondary school") her children attend. She tends to be more open and reasonable, oftentimes when it comes to the children's wrongdoings but can be stern as well. She and Stef legally marry, and the discussion of Lena carrying her first child arises. Lena interviews for a promotion at work and reveals she is pregnant, leading the panel to question her ability to balance work and home. She later develops [Pre-eclampsia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-eclampsia "Pre-eclampsia"), which leads to a [miscarriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miscarriage "Miscarriage").
*   Callie Adams Foster (formerly Callie Quinn Jacob) ([Maia Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maia_Mitchell "Maia Mitchell"))[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast2-5) is the adoptive daughter of Stef and Lena, adoptive sister to Brandon, Mariana, and Jesus, and maternal half-sister to Jude. In the pilot episode, the court places Callie in the Adams Foster home after serving time in juvenile detention for damaging her abusive foster father's property. Later, with Brandon's help, she goes to get her younger half-brother Jude (then believed to be her brother), who is still in the abusive foster home. Callie quickly develops a crush on Brandon before Jude becomes furious at her after seeing them kiss at Stef and Lena's wedding. Fearing the court will place her back into foster care, Callie attempts to run away, where she ends up eating food at a gas station without paying. This leads her into a temporary group home to counsel her actions and keep her away from Brandon. As time passes, Callie and Brandon hold back their feelings for each other. Callie's adoption is initially put on hold after the discovery that she and Jude do not share the same birth father. Later, Robert Quinn, who reveals himself to be Callie's birth father, approaches Callie. Robert introduces her to his family, and she quickly bonds with his daughter, Sophia. After Robert feels ready to turn over his paternal rights, Sophia tears up the paperwork, hoping Callie feels the same way about their newfound sibling bond, which appears to be the exact opposite. Stef and Lena officially adopt her following a prolonged battle with the justice system and a passionate speech to the judge.
*   Mariana Adams Foster ([Cierra Ramirez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cierra_Ramirez "Cierra Ramirez"))[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3) is Stef and Lena's adoptive daughter, Jesus' twin sister, younger adoptive sister to Brandon and Callie, and Jude's older adoptive sister. Mariana is an intelligent teenage girl who likes to involve herself in whatever she finds enjoyable, particularly when she is social with her friends and gossips at school. She is also very proficient at coding and mathematics. Like many teenage girls, Mariana struggles with her self-confidence, heritage, and appearance, as seen when she dyes her hair blond to fit in. She dances, acts, sings, and eventually forms her own dance team before becoming the lead actress in Brandon's senior project musical. Mariana initially supports her birth mother financially by selling Jesus' ADHD medication at school. Jesus confronts their birth mom to no longer contact Mariana, only to also rope in Brandon, which causes him financial and physical harm, for which she is apologetic. Later, Mariana hopes to change her image, joins the dance team, and takes a liking toward one of Brandon's bandmates. She is very close to Jesus, but they often tease each other.
*   Jesus Adams Foster ([Jake T. Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jake_T._Austin "Jake T. Austin") in seasons 1–2, [Noah Centineo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noah_Centineo "Noah Centineo") in seasons 3–5)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast2-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-6) is Stef and Lena's adoptive son, twin brother to Mariana, and adoptive sibling to Brandon, Callie, and Jude. He has [ADHD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ADHD "ADHD") and joins the wrestling team in an effort to offset the negative effects of his medication through the advice of Mike. Jesus loves his twin sister, Mariana, and the pair share resentment toward their biological mother. He is a womanizer at first, having a short string of romantic relationships and sometimes charming his mothers, including when he covers up for Mariana's wrongdoings. But he is now more respectful after getting back together with Emma. Jesus feels as though he has no involvement in Mariana's [quinceañera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincea%C3%B1era "Quinceañera") preparations but later opts to be her escort in an effort to be at their birthday celebration. In the third season, Jesus temporarily resides at a boarding school for his high school wrestling team but returns after Callie's adoption. After he admits to his parents that he was taking [steroids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steroids "Steroids") while away at boarding school, Stef and Lena no longer allow Jesus to participate on the wrestling team at Anchor Beach. Jesus later suffers a [TBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traumatic_brain_injury "Traumatic brain injury") after accidentally shooting himself in the head with a nail gun, which affects his personality and his academic performance.
*   Jude Adams Foster (formerly Jude Jacob) ([Hayden Byerly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayden_Byerly "Hayden Byerly"))[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast2-5) is the youngest Adams Foster child, he is Callie's half brother, and he is also Brandon, Jesus, and Mariana's adoptive sibling. Callie rescues Jude from their abusive foster father's house. As Jude settles into his new home, Mariana paints his nails blue and Callie tells him to wash it off but then learns to accept Jude's choices. At school, he quickly becomes friends with a kind-hearted boy, Connor, and as their friendship grows, Jude begins [questioning his sexual orientation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Questioning_(sexuality_and_gender) "Questioning (sexuality and gender)").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Hollywood_Life-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Hollywood.com-8) When Connor's father suspects Jude's feelings, he forbids the boys from seeing each other outside of school. Jude slips into a phase of [selective mutism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selective_mutism "Selective mutism"), a [social anxiety disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_anxiety_disorder "Social anxiety disorder") where he does not speak entirely for a certain extent of time in fear of embarrassment, only to finally open up to Callie about his feelings. Jude and Connor kiss and begin dating, but Jude refuses to label himself as gay. After seeing how badly this affects Connor at an LGBTQ dance in season 3, he [comes out as gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_out "Coming out"). At the end of the first season, Stef and Lena legally adopt Jude. Following Callie's own adoption, Jude admits he is in love with Connor, who returns the sentiment. After Connor moves to [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles") to live with his mom and because their long-distance relationship does not work out very well, they break up, and he later dates a new friend, Noah. Jude finally graduates from ABCC and gets into the College of Arts and Letters, UCLA. He and Noah maintain their relationship throughout their high school years, but break up when Noah goes to university, although they remain good friends.
*   Brandon Foster ([David Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lambert_(actor) "David Lambert (actor)"))[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast2-5) is the eldest Foster child, biological son of Stef and Mike, and older adoptive brother to Jesus and Mariana, as well as to Callie and Jude. Brandon has an infatuation for Callie but after his biological mother and father place a [restraining order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restraining_order "Restraining order") against him, and despite he and Callie having sex the night before her adoption, they later resist further temptations to proceed with their relationship. Brandon also has a talent for music, excelling in piano, and is on the verge of entering a highly distinguished music program. After raising money to obtain fake IDs to get into a bar (as he is legally underage), Brandon is beat up by his dealer. Following his subsequent hospitalization, Brandon loses sensation in his hand, causing him to miss his spot in the music program. Still able to play the piano, he joins a band. In the third season, Brandon goes to the Idylwild band camp and competes to play at [Disney Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disney_Hall "Disney Hall"), where he wins the competition. During his senior year of high school, he receives an acceptance letter into [The Juilliard School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Juilliard_School "The Juilliard School"), his top choice in colleges and among the most prestigious in music and the arts. Later, however, Brandon is [academically dismissed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academically_dismissed "Academically dismissed") from ever attending college as a student discloses bribing Brandon to take his [scholastic assessment test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SAT "SAT").
*   Mike Foster ([Danny Nucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Nucci "Danny Nucci"))[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast-3)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-cast2-5) is Stef's patrol partner and ex-husband as well as Brandon's father. He makes a number of appearances in the Adams Foster home, especially when it involves seeing Brandon. When searching for Jesus in the twins' birth mother's home, Mike witnesses Ana's boyfriend shooting Stef and, in turn, Mike fires at the shooter. Mike hadn't noticed the shooter dropped the gun and still shot him, which Stef witnessed, forcing her to hide the truth to protect Mike. He later learns that the money he gives his son for piano lessons is used to bribe Ana to lie in court so Mike does not lose his job. This only complicates the issue as the court abruptly determines that Mike is not guilty before Ana even has the chance to testify. Mike is also a recovering alcoholic, attends [Alcoholics Anonymous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholics_Anonymous "Alcoholics Anonymous") meetings, and retains a live-in girlfriend, Dani, who helps maintain his sobriety. The pair break up when she is sent to prison for [statutory rape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statutory_rape "Statutory rape") with an already sober Brandon. Mike and Ana soon begin a romantic relationship and get engaged in season 5 and the two got married during the time jump; he also becomes the step-father of Bella. Mike was also the foster father to AJ Hensdale.

He starts to date Mariana a couple of days or months after he took her virginity while she was dating Mat. He appears in season five being toyed by Mariana in a few episodes.

*   Dani (Danielle) Kirkland ([Marla Sokoloff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marla_Sokoloff "Marla Sokoloff")) is Mike's girlfriend whom he met at AA. Brandon, later, discloses to his parents and step-mother that after returning to his father's house drunk one night, Dani took advantage of and had sex with him. ## Production

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Production")]

### Conception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Conception")]

_The Fosters_ was originally conceived by [openly gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Openly_gay "Openly gay") creators Bradley Bredeweg and [Peter Paige](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Paige "Peter Paige")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-TheBacklot1-11) who wanted to write a drama that reflected the "modern American family". After originally considering a story about two gay fathers, the pair decided the subject of two men raising a family had already been done on television and began to instead consider a story about two women.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HuffPostGV1-12) When asked about the concept of two lesbian mothers raising a blended family, Bredeweg stated, "We realized that there was a kind of a vacuum when it came to stories about women raising families. So we set off in that direction. Many of our own friends are moms raising biological kids. Some of them have fostered and adopted. Suddenly, we realized that we had a story here that hadn't been told on television before."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HuffPostGV1-12) Additionally, certain elements of the series which deal with the foster care system are said to have been inspired by a troubled childhood friend of Bredeweg, who struggled in the foster system before eventually being adopted in her senior year of high school.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HuffPostGV1-12)

### Development

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Development")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c3/Jennifer_Lopez_at_GLAAD_Media_Awards.jpg/250px-Jennifer_Lopez_at_GLAAD_Media_Awards.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jennifer_Lopez_at_GLAAD_Media_Awards.jpg)

Executive producer [Jennifer Lopez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Lopez "Jennifer Lopez")

When developing the concept, Bredeweg and Paige were initially met with some resistance from Hollywood, with Bredeweg recounting, "[T]here were some people around us, some people in town who said, 'You know, it is just not going to happen. You are never going to sell this show.'" After completing the first draft of the pilot script, the team was introduced to [Jennifer Lopez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jennifer_Lopez "Jennifer Lopez") through a friend who worked at her production company [Nuyorican Productions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuyorican_Productions "Nuyorican Productions"), which was looking to branch out into scripted television. When describing their initial pitch to Lopez, Bredeweg stated, "When we met with Jennifer, she really fell in love with it. The moment we had her, we knew that we had a force behind us."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HuffPostGV1-12)

Lopez's decision to become involved in the project is said to have been largely inspired by her late Aunt Marisa, Lopez's mother's gay elder sister who had faced discrimination during her lifetime due to her sexual orientation and was unable to have a family of her own.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HollywoodReporter2-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-UsWeekly-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-EntertainmentTonight-15) When discussing the show's concept, Lopez stated, "Although [the script] was about a non-traditional family and had some newer themes, it had some really basic themes as well about family and love and what's really important. And life can be complicated and messy sometimes and not simple. It gives a really good depiction of family in this day and age."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-EntertainmentTonight-15)

With Lopez on board, the team took the concept to several networks, including ABC Family, with Bredeweg recalling, "ABC Family was really receptive from the very beginning. Strangely, it felt a little like a match made in heaven. I mean, their slogan is 'A new kind of family.' We had a new kind of modern family, and it took off from there."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HuffPostGV1-12) On July 6, 2012, _[The Hollywood Reporter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Hollywood\_Reporter "The Hollywood Reporter"),_ among other sources, reported that Jennifer Lopez and her production company, Nuyorican Productions, were developing the yet-to-be-titled hour-long drama for ABC Family, with Lopez set to executive produce alongside [Simon Fields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Fields "Simon Fields") and Greg Gugliotta, as well as [showrunners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Showrunner "Showrunner") and head writers Peter Paige and Brad Bredeweg.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-17)

Finally, the first televised promo appeared on ABC Family on April 19, 2013.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Philly-18)

### Casting

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Casting")]

On August 23, 2012, sources reported that ABC Family had ordered a pilot for _The Fosters_, a series which would tell the story of a lesbian couple raising a "21st-century" multi-ethnic mix of foster and biological children.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HollywoodReporter3-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-21) On September 24, 2012, it was reported that [Teri Polo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teri_Polo "Teri Polo") and [Sherri Saum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherri_Saum "Sherri Saum") had been cast to star in the pilot as the two leads, Stef Adams Foster and Lena Adams Foster, respectively.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Deadline.com1-22) It is worth noting that neither are openly members of the LGBTQ+ community.

On February 6, 2013, it was reported that ABC Family had picked up the show, with production set to begin that spring for a summer 2013 premiere. The rest of the principal cast was also announced at that time, including [Danny Nucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danny_Nucci "Danny Nucci") as Stef's ex-husband Mike Foster, [David Lambert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Lambert_(actor) "David Lambert (actor)") as their biological son Brandon Foster, [Jake T. Austin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jake_T._Austin "Jake T. Austin") and [Cierra Ramirez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cierra_Ramirez "Cierra Ramirez") as Stef and Lena's twins Jesus and Mariana Foster, and [Maia Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maia_Mitchell "Maia Mitchell") and [Hayden Byerly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayden_Byerly "Hayden Byerly") as their foster children Callie and Jude Jacob.

When recounting the casting process, Bredeweg explained, "[W]e spent tireless hours trying to find the right person for each role. Then they all began to line up—it was like dominos—the moment we found our Lena, the moment we found our Callie, the moment we found our Stef, it sort of all started to line up perfectly for us."[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-HuffPostGV1-12) On April 11, 2013, _[TV Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV\_Guide "TV Guide")_ unveiled the first official cast photo of _The Fosters_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-23)

In March 2015, it was announced that Jake T. Austin would be leaving the show. He tweeted: "I'm honored to have been a part of such a groundbreaking series, but I personally want to let you know that my time on the show has come to an end. Thank you for letting me be a part of your family, it's been a pleasure." It was announced three months later that [Noah Centineo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noah_Centineo "Noah Centineo") would replace Austin in the role of Jesus.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-AccessHollywood1-24)

## Broadcast

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Broadcast")]

_The Fosters_ premiered on June 3, 2013, and ran for ten episodes. On July 30, 2013, the series was picked up for a full season[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-25) and an additional eleven episodes were produced,[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-extraepisodes-26) with the first season returning on January 13, 2014, before concluding on March 24. On October 11, 2013, ABC Family renewed _The Fosters_ for a second season[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-secondhalfpremiere-29) that premiered on June 16, 2014. The summer finale premiered on August 18, 2014. In July, ABC Family announced a Christmas special to premiere in December with the second half of season 2 to premiere in January 2015. The third season premiered on June 8, 2015.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-S3P-30)

On January 13, 2015, ABC Family renewed the series for a third season which premiered on June 8,[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-S3P-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-31) with the second half set to premiere on January 18, 2016, on _Freeform_.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-32) On November 24, 2015, the premiere date was pushed to a week later on January 25, 2016.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-33) On November 30, 2015, ABC Family announced that _The Fosters_ was renewed for a fourth season and began airing on June 20, 2016.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-34)

While Canada broadcasts the series on [ABC Spark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_Spark "ABC Spark"), it airs on [Fox8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox8 "Fox8") in Australia where its second season premiered on February 3, 2015.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-35) In Turkey, the series airs on _Dizimax Drama_.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-36)

On January 10, 2017, The Fosters was renewed for a fifth season, which included the series' 100th episode.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-37)

On January 3, 2018, Freeform announced that _The Fosters_ was ending after five seasons. The show's two-hour 100th episode acted as a Season 5 finale, setting up the three-part limited series event that aired in June 2018. The three-episode finale will introduce a spin-off series centered around Maia Mitchell's Callie and Cierra Ramirez's Mariana.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-38)

## Reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Reception")]

### Critical reception

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Critical reception")]

On the [review aggregator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Review_aggregator "Review aggregator") website [Rotten Tomatoes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotten_Tomatoes "Rotten Tomatoes"), _The Fosters_ received an overall score of 98%.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-40) On [Metacritic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metacritic "Metacritic"), the first season of the show holds a score of 69 out of 100, based on twelve reviews, indicating "generally favorable reviews".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Metacritic-41)

While acknowledging its network was somewhat beholden to the "soapy" format its target demographic had become accustomed to, critics praised the series for its ability to appeal to adults and younger viewers alike, with _[Boston Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston\_Herald "Boston Herald")_ critic Mark A. Perigard writing, "The show cannily plays to teen hopes and dreams [...] but there's story for the adults as well."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-BostonHerald-42)_[St. Louis Post-Dispatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St.\_Louis\_Post-Dispatch "St. Louis Post-Dispatch")_ critic Gail Pennington echoed the sentiment, writing "Intelligent enough for adults, accessible enough for younger viewers and entertaining enough for both."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Post-Dispatch-43)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Sherri_Saum_and_Teri_Polo.jpg/330px-Sherri_Saum_and_Teri_Polo.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sherri_Saum_and_Teri_Polo.jpg)

Series stars Sherri Saum and Teri Polo

The series has garnered positive reception for its innovative portrayal of [LGBT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT "LGBT") characters and themes. _[Entertainment Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Entertainment\_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")_ critic, Sarah Caldwell wrote that "[s]eeing a lesbian, biracial couple on a family TV show is a big deal. [I]f you look at the demographics of most TV shows, it's easy to realize how important, and deliberate, this choice was."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-EntertainmentWeekly-44)_[Philadelphia Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia\_Daily\_News "Philadelphia Daily News")_ critic Ellen Gray wrote, "Stef and Lena [are] the kind of parents I've met more in real life than on television. I hope they'll be as welcome there as they seem to be welcoming."[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Philly.com-45)[TV Guide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV_Guide "TV Guide") critic Matt Rousch felt similarly, writing, "there's something refreshing about its unforced approach to redefining what a family looks like."[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-TV_Guide-46) In addition to its adult characters, the series garnered praise for its handling of 13-year-old Jude's [questioning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Questioning_(sexuality_and_gender) "Questioning (sexuality and gender)") of his [sexual orientation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_orientation "Sexual orientation"), with [Hollywood.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hollywood.com "Hollywood.com") citing Byerly's "heartwarming" portrayal when naming Jude to its list of "Favorite LGBTQ Characters on TV" in 2014.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Hollywood.com-8) The LGBT advocacy organization [GLAAD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLAAD "GLAAD") and gay-interest media outlet [TheBacklot.com](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TheBacklot.com "TheBacklot.com") also commended the show's decision to introduce the character of [transgender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender "Transgender") teenager Cole, portrayed by transgender actor Tom Phelan, in the second half of its first season.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-TheBacklot1-11)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-GLAAD1-47)

In his review of the pilot episode, _[Variety's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety\_(magazine) "Variety (magazine)")_ Brian Lowry criticized what he felt were formulaic elements, writing that what was distinctive about the series appeared to have been "extracted during the pitch meeting, indicating a show either built by committee or incorporating too many notes." Although acknowledging that Polo and Saum were competent actresses and that the show "had its heart in the right place", Lowry described the series as an "utterly by-the-numbers affair".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Variety1-48)_[PopMatters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PopMatters "PopMatters")_ critic Maysa Hattab detected some of the same problems, writing "_[T]he Fosters_ feel less like a family than a careful assembly of machine-tooled parts, as if the show were engineered for a focus group approved 'family drama' category", while conceding that the lead characters, Stef and Lena were "a likeable pair".[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-PopMatters-49)

#### Controversy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Controversy")]

On October 8, 2012, more than seven months prior to the series debut, the socially conservative [One Million Moms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Million_Moms "One Million Moms") organization, a division of the [American Family Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Family_Association "American Family Association"), condemned Lopez and the show, encouraging audiences to boycott it.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-EntertainmentWeekly2-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-ABC-51) The group, which has routinely advocated against the depiction of same-sex couples in the media, stated: "While foster care and adoption is a wonderful thing and the Bible does teach us to help orphans, this program is attempting to redefine marriage and family by having two moms raise these children together."[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-53) They issued the following statement:

Obviously, ABC has lost their minds. They haven't let up so neither will we. ABC's Family Channel has several anti-family programs, and they are planning on adding to that growing list. ABC Family has approved a series pilot from Jennifer Lopez's production company, Nuyorican, about a lesbian couple and their diverse family.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-ABC-51)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-55)
In response, ABC defended the television show, with ABC Family President [Michael Riley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Riley "Michael Riley") countering that _The Fosters_ merges perfectly with the network's "groundbreaking storytelling and iconic characters" and will feature "the same depth, heart, close relationships and authenticity that our viewers have come to expect".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-56) Other sources have also defended the show. Josh Middleton, a writer from _[Philadelphia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia\_(magazine) "Philadelphia (magazine)")_ magazine, called One Million Moms' statement "silliness" as well as "ridiculous" and said, "They obviously missed the boat on shows like _[Modern Family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern\_Family "Modern Family")_ and _[The New Normal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Normal\_(TV\_series) "The New Normal (TV series)")_, which have been on air—and killing it in the ratings game—for a while now".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-Philly-18)

## Spin-off

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Spin-off")]

Main article: [_Good Trouble_ (TV series)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Trouble_(TV_series) "Good Trouble (TV series)")

On January 3, 2018, following the announcement of the ending of the series, Freeform announced a spin-off was in the works. It would center the lives of Callie and Mariana Adams Foster, now living in Los Angeles, a few years after the series finale of _The Fosters_, which contains a five-year time jump. The spin-off was given a 13-episode order.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-86) On May 23, 2018, it was announced that the title of the spin-off series was _Good Trouble_.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-87) On February 5, 2019, it was announced via Twitter that the show has been renewed for a second season.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-88) On January 17, 2020, the series has been renewed for a third season.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-S3Renewal-89) The renewal for the fourth season was announced on September 8, 2021. The fourth season premiered on March 9, 2022 on freeform, and on March 10 on Hulu.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Fosters_(American_TV_series)#cite_note-90) The fifth and final season aired in two parts.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

_[The Fosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Fosters\_(American\_TV\_series) "The Fosters (American TV series)")_ is an American drama series which aired on [Freeform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freeform_(TV_channel) "Freeform (TV channel)") (formerly ABC Family) from June 3, 2013, to June 6, 2018.

A total of 104 episodes were broadcast over five seasons.
